column1: What does machine learning say about the drivers of inflation? (BIS WP on arXiv)

The thesis titled What does machine learning say about the drivers of inflation? by Emanuel Kohlscheen  published as BIS Working Paper No. 980  explores the factors influencing Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation using a machine learning approach. The study focuses on 20 advanced economies over the period from 2000 to 2021  employing a computationally intensive method involving 1 000 regression trees based on six key macroeconomic variables. This data-driven  non-parametric method  specifically the random forest technique  is used to predict inflation outcomes and assess the role of various drivers  including inflation expectations  past inflation  oil prices  and the output gap.

The paper highlights the superior predictive performance of the machine learning model compared to traditional econometric models  as evidenced by lower out-of-sample root mean square errors (RMSE). The findings underscore the significance of expectations in determining inflation outcomes  although their influence has diminished over the past decade. The study also notes that exchange rate variations contribute minimally to inflation predictions.

The research contributes to the growing body of literature applying machine learning to economic prediction  demonstrating the method's effectiveness in capturing non-linear relationships in inflation dynamics. The results support the importance of expectations in inflation targeting frameworks and emphasize the role of non-linearities in the relationship between macroeconomic variables and inflation. Additionally  the study identifies oil prices and global producer price index (PPI) inflation as significant global drivers of CPI inflation  particularly after 2010.

The paper is structured as follows: Section 1 introduces the research questions and the relevance of understanding inflation drivers. Section 2 details the methodology and dataset used for predicting inflation. Section 3 presents the baseline results  highlighting the performance of the random forest model. Section 4 discusses the changing importance of inflation drivers over time. The study concludes by reaffirming the utility of machine learning in economic analysis and its potential to enhance understanding of inflation dynamics.
